newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD puts tax demands in writing to Kohl.
newsitem.headline: German SPD puts tax demands in writing to Kohl.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats on Wednesday sent Chancellor Helmut Kohl a letter setting out their conditions for a resumption of talks with the coalition government on sweeping tax reforms.
Chief whip Peter Struck confirmed a newspaper report that the SPD wanted a two-point cut in unemployment and pensions insurance contributions from July 1 of this year.
And, in a change of position, he said the SPD was prepared to raise value added tax as well as petrol tax to compensate for the extra costs to the budget of slashing occupational insurance charges.
The SPD has also said it wants a big cut in taxes from the start of 1998 which would benefit ordinary workers and their families and kick-start economic demand.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Tuesday he would answer the SPD's letter on Wednesday and seek further contacts this week to restart talks on taxes broken off nearly two weeks ago following a row over government cuts in coal subsidies.
But the SPD position looks to be far away from Waigel's plan to cut 30 billion marks in corporate and income taxes by 1999.

Kohl's cabinet on Tuesday cleared Waigel's 1998 tax bill, which would cut both corporate and commercial income tax rates to a unified 40 percent, as well as knocking two points off the 7.5 percent solidarity income tax surcharge.
The bill, which would lighten the tax burden by 7.5 billion marks, would pave the way for big cuts in the bottom and top rates of income tax, and a further round of corporate tax cuts in 1999.
Coalition parties are expected to introduce the tax bill to parliament this Friday.
